atoms.text: This guide describes how to let the GateLog delivery service write load balancer access logs into a storage bucket named lb-access-logs-prod. The bucket and the IAM role that GateLog assumes, GateLogDeliveryRole, both belong to account 111111111111. GateLog writes one gzip-compressed log file every five minutes under the prefix gatelog/year/month/day/. Because the bucket and the role share an account, the grant is made entirely in the role's identity-based policy, and the bucket policy is left unchanged. Attach a policy to GateLogDeliveryRole that allows storage:PutObject on arn:storage:::lb-access-logs-prod/gatelog/* and storage:GetBucketLocation on arn:storage:::lb-access-logs-prod. Do not add a statement for the role to the bucket policy; an existing bucket policy without a matching allow does not block same-account access unless it contains an explicit deny. Confirm that the role's trust policy lists the GateLog service principal so the service can assume the role. In the GateLog console, enter the bucket name and prefix, then choose Validate to have the service write a test object named gatelog-validation.txt. If validation returns AccessDenied, check the resource ARN in the role policy and look for explicit deny statements in the bucket policy.

This guide describes how to let the GateLog delivery service write load balancer access logs into a storage bucket named lb-access-logs-prod. The bucket belongs to account 222222222222, while the IAM role that GateLog assumes, GateLogDeliveryRole, belongs to account 111111111111. GateLog writes one gzip-compressed log file every five minutes under the prefix gatelog/year/month/day/. Because the role is in a different account, the bucket owner grants access by adding a statement to the bucket policy that names the role as principal. The statement uses the principal arn:iam::111111111111:role/GateLogDeliveryRole and allows storage:PutObject on arn:storage:::lb-access-logs-prod/gatelog/* and storage:GetBucketLocation on arn:storage:::lb-access-logs-prod. The role's own policy in account 111111111111 must also allow those two actions on the same resources. Confirm that the role's trust policy lists the GateLog service principal so the service can assume the role. In the GateLog console, enter the bucket name and prefix, then choose Validate to have the service write a test object named gatelog-validation.txt. If validation returns AccessDenied, check the principal ARN in the bucket policy and look for explicit deny statements in either policy.

This guide covers delivery of audit trail events from the TrailKeeper service to a storage bucket named org-audit-trails. The bucket and the IAM role TrailKeeperWriter are both in account 333333333333. TrailKeeper batches management events into JSON files and writes them every 15 minutes under the prefix trails/events/. Access is granted only through the identity-based policy on TrailKeeperWriter, and the bucket policy is not modified. Add a policy to the role that allows storage:PutObject on arn:storage:::org-audit-trails/trails/events/* and storage:GetBucketAcl on arn:storage:::org-audit-trails. TrailKeeper checks the bucket ACL permission before its first write, so omitting it causes the trail to report a configuration error. Do not edit the bucket policy, since same-account access through the role policy is sufficient when no deny statement applies. Create the trail in the TrailKeeper console and select the role as the delivery identity. After about 15 minutes, list the trails/events/ prefix and verify that a JSON file has appeared. If no file appears, review the trail status page for the most recent delivery error.

This guide covers delivery of audit trail events from the TrailKeeper service to a storage bucket named org-audit-trails. The bucket is owned by account 444444444444, and the IAM role TrailKeeperWriter is in account 333333333333. TrailKeeper batches management events into JSON files and writes them every 15 minutes under the prefix trails/events/. The bucket owner grants access by adding a bucket policy statement whose principal is arn:iam::333333333333:role/TrailKeeperWriter. That statement allows storage:PutObject on arn:storage:::org-audit-trails/trails/events/* and storage:GetBucketAcl on arn:storage:::org-audit-trails. TrailKeeper checks the bucket ACL permission before its first write, so omitting it causes the trail to report a configuration error. The role's identity-based policy in account 333333333333 must allow the same two actions on those resources. Create the trail in the TrailKeeper console and select the role as the delivery identity. After about 15 minutes, the bucket owner can list the trails/events/ prefix and verify that a JSON file has appeared. If no file appears, review the trail status page for the most recent delivery error.

This guide explains how to configure EdgeCache to deliver CDN request logs into a storage bucket named cdn-request-logs. The bucket and the IAM role EdgeCacheLogRole are in account 555555555555. EdgeCache writes log files every ten minutes and partitions them by distribution ID, using keys of the form cdn/DISTRIBUTION_ID/date/file.log.gz. The grant is made only in the identity-based policy of EdgeCacheLogRole, and the bucket policy stays as it is. Write the policy so that storage:PutObject is allowed on arn:storage:::cdn-request-logs/cdn/*, which covers every distribution under the cdn/ prefix. Add storage:ListBucket on arn:storage:::cdn-request-logs with a condition limiting the listed prefix to cdn/, because EdgeCache lists existing keys to avoid overwriting files. Leave the bucket policy untouched, as no bucket-level statement is required for a same-account role. In the EdgeCache console, open the distribution's logging settings, choose the bucket, and set the prefix to cdn/. Request a few test objects through the distribution and check the bucket for a new compressed file within ten minutes. If files are missing, verify the prefix in the policy matches the prefix in the logging settings.

This guide explains how to configure EdgeCache to deliver CDN request logs into a storage bucket named cdn-request-logs. The bucket is owned by account 666666666666, and the IAM role EdgeCacheLogRole is in account 555555555555. EdgeCache writes log files every ten minutes and partitions them by distribution ID, using keys of the form cdn/DISTRIBUTION_ID/date/file.log.gz. The bucket owner grants access by adding a statement to the bucket policy with the principal arn:iam::555555555555:root, so that roles in the other account can be authorized. That statement allows storage:PutObject on arn:storage:::cdn-request-logs/cdn/*, which covers every distribution under the cdn/ prefix. It also allows storage:ListBucket on arn:storage:::cdn-request-logs with a condition limiting the listed prefix to cdn/, because EdgeCache lists existing keys to avoid overwriting files. The identity-based policy on EdgeCacheLogRole in account 555555555555 must allow the same actions. In the EdgeCache console, open the distribution's logging settings, choose the bucket, and set the prefix to cdn/. Request a few test objects through the distribution and check the bucket for a new compressed file within ten minutes. If files are missing, verify the prefix in the bucket policy matches the prefix in the logging settings.

This guide describes delivery of virtual network flow records from the NetFlowLens service to a storage bucket named netflow-records. The bucket and the IAM role NetFlowLensDelivery are in account 777777777777. NetFlowLens writes one plain-text file per network interface group every minute under the prefix flows/. Objects must be written with server-side encryption using a customer-managed key, so the policy carries a condition on the encryption header. In the identity-based policy of NetFlowLensDelivery, allow storage:PutObject on arn:storage:::netflow-records/flows/* only when the request header for server-side encryption equals the value your organization requires. Because the bucket and role share an account, the bucket policy is not changed and does not need a statement for this role. Also grant the role use of the encryption key in the key's own policy or the role policy, according to your key management practice. Enable flow records in the NetFlowLens console and point the destination at the bucket and the flows/ prefix. Within a few minutes, confirm that new objects appear and that their metadata shows the expected encryption setting. Requests that omit the header are rejected with AccessDenied.

NetFlowLens writes one plain-text file per network interface group every minute under the prefix flows/. Objects must be written with server-side encryption using a customer-managed key, so the grant carries a condition on the encryption header. The bucket owner adds a bucket policy statement with the principal arn:iam::777777777777:role/NetFlowLensDelivery that allows storage:PutObject on arn:storage:::netflow-records/flows/* only when the server-side encryption header equals the required value. The role's identity-based policy in its own account must allow the same action on the same resources. Also grant the role use of the encryption key in the key's own policy, according to your key management practice. Enable flow records in the NetFlowLens console and point the destination at the bucket and the flows/ prefix. Within a few minutes, the bucket owner can confirm that new objects appear and that their metadata shows the expected encryption setting. Requests that omit the header are rejected with AccessDenied.

This guide covers exporting database query logs from the QueryLedger service to a storage bucket named db-query-archive. The bucket and the IAM role QueryLedgerExport belong to account 121212121212. QueryLedger uploads one gzip-compressed log file per database instance every hour under the prefix ledger/instance-id/. Large files are uploaded with multipart upload, so the role needs more than a single write permission. In the identity-based policy of QueryLedgerExport, allow storage:PutObject, storage:AbortMultipartUpload, and storage:ListMultipartUploadParts on arn:storage:::db-query-archive/ledger/*. Add storage:ListBucketMultipartUploads on arn:storage:::db-query-archive so interrupted uploads can be found and resumed. No change is made to the bucket policy, because the role and bucket are in the same account. Register the bucket and prefix in the QueryLedger export settings and select the role. Trigger a manual export and confirm that a completed object, not just parts, is present under the prefix. If uploads stall, check that the abort and list permissions are present, as they are required for cleanup.

A second action, storage:ListBucketMultipartUploads on arn:storage:::db-query-archive, lets interrupted uploads be found and resumed. The role's identity-based policy in account 121212121212 must allow the same actions. Register the bucket and prefix in the QueryLedger export settings and select the role. Trigger a manual export and confirm that a completed object, not just parts, is present under the prefix. If uploads stall, check that the abort and list permissions are present in the bucket policy, as they are required for cleanup.

This guide describes how to give a log processing role read access to files that the PodScribe service delivers into a storage bucket named container-logs. The bucket and the IAM role LogParserRole are in account 565656565656. PodScribe writes container log files under the prefix pods/namespace/, and a parser job assuming LogParserRole reads each new file and then deletes it. The write side is already configured, so this procedure covers only the reader. Grant access in the identity-based policy of LogParserRole, and leave the bucket policy unchanged. The policy should allow storage:GetObject and storage:DeleteObject on arn:storage:::container-logs/pods/*. It should also allow storage:ListBucket on arn:storage:::container-logs with a prefix condition of pods/. Check the bucket policy only for explicit deny statements, since an allow statement is not needed for a same-account role. Run the parser job once against a single namespace prefix. Verify that the job lists and reads a file and that the file is removed afterward. A 403 response on listing usually means the prefix condition does not match the requested prefix.

This guide covers delivery of DNS query logs from the ResolverLog service to a storage bucket named dns-query-logs. The bucket and the IAM role ResolverLogWriter are in account 909090909090. ResolverLog writes newline-delimited JSON files every five minutes under resolver/zone-id/year/month/day/. The bucket has a lifecycle rule that expires objects under resolver/ after 90 days, and this does not affect the access configuration. Access is granted only by the identity-based policy of ResolverLogWriter, and the bucket policy is not modified. The policy allows storage:PutObject on arn:storage:::dns-query-logs/resolver/* and storage:GetBucketLocation on arn:storage:::dns-query-logs. It does not grant storage:DeleteObject, so the role cannot remove files that it has already delivered. In the ResolverLog console, create a log configuration for the zone and select the bucket, the prefix resolver/, and the role. Send a few test queries to the zone and wait for the next five-minute interval. Confirm that a JSON file exists under the zone's prefix and contains the test queries. If the configuration stays in a pending state, check that the role's trust policy names the ResolverLog service.

This guide describes how to let the MailRelay service deliver message delivery logs to a storage bucket named mail-delivery-logs, using a dedicated IAM user for services that cannot assume roles. The bucket and the IAM user relay-log-writer are in account 454545454545. MailRelay writes one CSV file per hour under the prefix relay/ and overwrites a small index file named relay/_latest.json after each upload. Access is granted only by an identity-based policy attached to relay-log-writer, and the bucket policy is unchanged. The policy allows storage:PutObject on arn:storage:::mail-delivery-logs/relay/* and storage:GetObject on arn:storage:::mail-delivery-logs/relay/_latest.json. The read permission is limited to the index file, because MailRelay reads it only to find the last uploaded hour. Create an access key for the user and enter it in the MailRelay log destination settings along with the bucket name and prefix. Because the user and the bucket share an account, no bucket policy statement is needed. After the next hour boundary, verify that a CSV file and an updated _latest.json exist under relay/. Rotate the access key on the schedule set by your security policy.
